title: COVID-19's myths, facts, concerning and obstinate posts on social network, and the mental health status of social network users in Bangladesh
screen_reason: Reports the share of users who spread misinformation: 89 of 1,200 Bangladeshi social-network users (7.4%) were found to have spread COVID-19 myths/misinformation, based on researchers' observation and verification of the participants' own publicly shared posts. Share of users who shared any misinformation from observed platform activity = SHARING (actor_share).

estimates.date: April to October 2021 (online questionnaire fielded 6 April - 6 August 2021, with concurrent observation of participants' public posts)
estimates.measure_type: % of studied social-network users whose observed public posts spread COVID-19 myths and misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 89/1200 (7.4%) 'Myths and misinformation spread'; for comparison 333/1200 (27.8%) 'Facts spread'
estimates.denominator: 1,200 active Bangladeshi social-network users who completed the online survey (of 1,809 who started it), recruited from the research team members' own social-network friend lists on the basis of having posted COVID-19-related content
estimates.definition: A participant counted in the numerator if at least one of their publicly shared COVID-19 posts was categorised as a myth, i.e. 'fallacious, irrelevant and fabricated information about COVID-19 ... any shared posts on social network spreading information that did not replicate a scientific fact or partially replicate scientifically validated information that might have caused potential misunderstandings'.
estimates.misinfo_def: "COVID-19's myths: fallacious, irrelevant and fabricated information about COVID-19 that were noticeably different from those that were conforming to scientific standards"; "the occurrence of anyone's fake or incorrect information sharing by unintentionally and unwittingly is called misinformation" (after Wardle).
estimates.source_quote: Of the 1200 respondents, 27.8% had spread facts related to COVID-19, 7.4% spread myths and misinformation.
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 8; Table 1 ('Myths and misinformation spread' 89, 7.4%), pp. 9-10; also Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Each participant's shared post was 'diligently scrutinized and reviewed by two competent researchers (both were pharmacists) who were unknown to the users'; content keywords were checked via the BuzzSumo content search, and veracity was compared against the WHO MythBusters page and against scientific journals and authoritative institutions (Bangladesh Ministry of Health, IEDCR, FDA, CDC, WHO). No inter-rater reliability statistic is reported for this classification (the Cronbach's alphas reported, 0.831-0.894, are for the DASS-21 and ISI psychometric scales, not for the post coding).
estimates.moderator_quote: Before conducting this study, the participants were selected from social network friends list of each of group members. Those persons on social networks were selected from their posts related to the corona virus or measures, suspected posts of myths and misinformation or facts, memes or trolls regarding COVID-19, concerning posts on COVID-19's scenarios.
estimates.notes: MAJOR denominator caveat: the sample is not a general population sample. Participants were drawn from the researchers' own social-network friend lists and were selected BECAUSE they had posted COVID-19 content, including 'suspected posts of myths and misinformation'. Selection on the outcome should push the estimate UP, yet the paper reports only 7.4%; either way the denominator is not interpretable as 'Bangladeshi social media users'. The sample is also heavily skewed (93.8% under 30, 75.3% male, 73.8% students, 68.7% graduates), and the Raosoft n=385 calculation implies a general-population frame that the recruitment does not deliver. CONSTRUCT CALL: I coded SHARING (actor_share) rather than RECALL because the Methods state the classification came from researchers observing and verifying participants' publicly shared posts ('we also concomitantly observed the publicly shared posts related to facts, myths, and hoax messages of COVID-19 ... upon taking consent'), and the consent text confirms observation ('we will only observe your publicly shared activities on your social networks'). The 'Independent variables' list describes the myths variable ambiguously ('myths and false information related to COVID-19 spread through social media by the respondent'), which could be read as self-report; if an adjudicator reads it that way the row becomes RECALL/sharing. Confidence medium for that reason.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) NOT extracted (not misinformation): 27.8% spread facts, 36.7% posted COVID-19 concerning posts, 28.1%/649 classified 'obstinate' (tours 16.8%, ceremonies 7.4%, get-togethers 8.3%, maskless group photos 26.4%, memes/trolls 21.7%). Memes and trolls are counted as 'obstinate', not as misinformation, by the authors, so I did not fold them into the numerator. Note the abstract's '28.1% ... shared obstinate' does not match any single Table 1 row; Table 3 splits the sample into 649 'obstinate people' (54.1%) and 551 'concerned people' (45.9%), so the abstract figure could not be reconciled with the tables and I did not extract it. 2) NOT extracted (demographic subgroups, not the headline): Table 3 gives myths spread by males 70/904 (7.7%), females 19/296 (6.4%), obstinate people 27/649 (4.2%) and concerned people 62/551 (11.3%), plus 'both facts and myths' 16 (1.77%) male / 2 (0.68%) female. 3) NOT extracted (within-misinformation composition, R3-adjacent but not a veracity share): Table 2 breaks the 89 myth-spreaders down by myth theme (wrong information about virus spreading 18/89 = 20.2%; false information about origin 15 = 16.9%; misinformation about treatment 14 = 15.7%; 'alcohol kills corona virus' 9 = 10.1%; misinformation about vaccines 7 = 7.9%). 4) NOT extracted: all mental-health prevalences (depression 43.9%, anxiety 30.9%, stress 23.8%, severe insomnia 2.8%) - outcomes, not misinformation. 5) DATA-QUALITY FLAG for the adjudicator: the Discussion states 'In our study, 31.8% of females shared facts on social platforms, while 26.4% of males spread myths and misinformation.' The 26.4% contradicts the paper's own Table 3 (males 70/904 = 7.7%) and matches instead the Table 1 'Group photo without mask' figure (26.4%); it appears to be an error in the Discussion, so I used the Table 1/Table 3 values. 6) NOT extracted: '12.5% of identified misinformation-related posts were acted upon by Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, and Twitter' - cited from the Centre for Countering Digital Hate, not this study's data.

rob.design: Cross-sectional online survey (Google Forms, Bengali, back-translated) of 1,200 Bangladeshi active social-network users, combined with researcher observation of the same participants' public posts. Recruitment: purposive, from the research team members' own social-network friend lists, selecting people who had posted COVID-19-related content (facts, suspected myths, memes/trolls, concern posts) or maskless-gathering photos; link distributed via Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram 6 April - 6 August 2021 (study window given elsewhere as April-October 2021). 1,809 started, 609 incomplete responses excluded, 1,200 analysed - a completion rate of 66.3%, but no true response rate is calculable because the invited pool is undefined. A Raosoft calculation (5% margin, 95% CI, population 45,000,000 social network users) gave a minimum of 385; the authors took 1,200. Post classification: two pharmacist researchers, blind to the users' identities, coded each observed post into four categories (myths / facts / obstinate / concerning), checking content via BuzzSumo and against WHO MythBusters, Bangladesh Ministry of Health, IEDCR, FDA and CDC sources; no reliability statistic reported for this coding. Mental health measured with DASS-21 and ISI (Cronbach's alpha 0.831-0.894). Analysis: frequencies, chi-square, and seemingly-unrelated multivariate logistic regression (RStudio, systemfit). Ethics approval CMR/EC/003, informed consent including explicit consent to observation of public posts. Author-declared limitations: few female respondents, no face-to-face interviewing, no post-pandemic comparison, unaddressed confounders.
